title: Best Things to Do in Osaka
excerpt: Neon-lit Dotonbori, street food, a castle, and big-city energy — here are the best things to do in Osaka for first-time visitors.
content:
Osaka is Japan's brash, fun-loving food capital — louder and more laid-back than Kyoto or Tokyo, and famous for eating well. It's an easy trip from Kyoto and a great addition to any Kansai itinerary. Here's what to do.

Dotonbori

Dotonbori is Osaka's neon heart — a canal-side strip blazing with giant illuminated signs (including the famous running-man billboard) and packed with restaurants and street food. It's the city's must-see, best experienced at night when the lights reflect off the water. Come hungry.

Eat the street food

Osaka is nicknamed "the nation's kitchen," and street food is the main event. Don't miss takoyaki (savory octopus balls) and okonomiyaki (a hearty savory pancake), both Osaka specialties. Kushikatsu (deep-fried skewers) is another local favorite. Eating your way through Dotonbori and the surrounding lanes is the quintessential Osaka experience.

Osaka Castle

Osaka Castle is the city's historic landmark, a striking reconstructed fortress set in a large park that's lovely for a stroll, especially in cherry blossom season. The museum inside covers the castle's dramatic history, and the top floor offers city views. A good daytime counterpoint to the neon nights.

More to do

  • Shinsekai: a retro, old-school district with a nostalgic atmosphere and the Tsutenkaku tower, great for kushikatsu.
  • Umeda Sky Building: a futuristic tower with a floating observation deck for panoramic views.
  • Kuromon Market: a covered market famous for fresh seafood and food stalls.
  • Theme parks: Osaka is home to a major world-famous theme park, a full-day draw for many visitors.
  • Nightlife: lively bars and entertainment, especially around Namba and Dotonbori.

How long to spend

Osaka works as a day trip from Kyoto (especially for an evening of food in Dotonbori) or as a one-to-two-day base of its own. Many travelers combine it with Kyoto and Nara into a Kansai loop. If food and energy are your thing, give it at least a full day and an evening.

Practical tips

  • Osaka is very walkable in its central districts, with an easy subway and loop line for longer hops.
  • Use your IC card for transit and even some food stalls.
  • Dotonbori is best at night; the castle and markets are daytime.
  • No tipping, as everywhere in Japan.

Bottom line

Osaka is where you come to eat, wander neon streets, and enjoy a more relaxed, exuberant side of urban Japan. Whether as a day trip or a short stay, it's a delicious and high-energy complement to the refined calm of nearby Kyoto.

title: teamLab in Tokyo: A Visitor's Guide
excerpt: teamLab's immersive digital art museums are among Tokyo's most popular experiences. Here's what to expect and how to plan your visit.
content:
teamLab is one of Tokyo's most extraordinary and popular experiences — an immersive digital art museum where rooms of light, color, and projection respond to your movement and presence. It's a favorite of nearly every first-time visitor, and unlike anything else you'll do in Japan. Here's how to make the most of it.

What it is

teamLab creates large-scale immersive digital art: you walk through dark halls filled with flowing projections, mirrored rooms of lights, interactive installations that change as you touch or move near them, and spaces designed to dissolve the boundary between you and the artwork. It's playful, beautiful, and genuinely mesmerizing for all ages.

Plan ahead: book timed tickets

The single most important tip: tickets are timed and sell out, often days or more in advance, especially on weekends and in peak travel seasons. Book your slot online ahead of time rather than hoping to walk up. Choose a time that fits your itinerary, and arrive a little early.

What to wear and bring

  • Wear comfortable clothing. Some installations have water features where you may walk through shallow water — check the specific exhibit's guidance, and consider shorts or rolled-up pants. There are often facilities for this.
  • Footwear: you may go barefoot in some areas; easy-off shoes help.
  • Avoid skirts in venues with mirrored floors.
  • Bring your phone or camera — it's extremely photogenic — but also take time to just experience it.

Who it's good for

teamLab is a hit with couples, families, kids, and anyone who enjoys art, photography, or just something wondrous and different. Children are usually delighted by the interactivity. It's accessible and not physically demanding, though it can be busy.

Practical tips

  • Allow a couple of hours to explore fully — don't rush it.
  • It can get crowded; weekday and earlier slots are often calmer.
  • Check the current location and exhibit details when booking, as venues and installations evolve over time.
  • Follow staff guidance on which rooms have water or special access rules.

Bottom line

teamLab is a Tokyo highlight that lives up to the hype — immersive, beautiful, and totally unique. Book your timed tickets in advance, wear something comfortable, and give yourself time to wander. It's an experience that stays with you long after the trip.

title: Best Free Things to Do in Japan
excerpt: Japan can be surprisingly affordable. Here are the best experiences — shrines, parks, markets, and views — that cost nothing.
content:
Japan has a reputation for being expensive, but some of its most memorable experiences are completely free. From ancient shrines to neon streets and sweeping views, here are the best things you can do without spending a yen.

Visit shrines (and many temples)

Most Shinto shrines are free to enter, including major ones. The spectacular Fushimi Inari in Kyoto, with its thousands of red torii gates, costs nothing, as does the serene Meiji Shrine in Tokyo. While many Buddhist temples charge a small entry fee for their main halls or gardens, you can often walk the grounds for free.

Wander the neighborhoods

Some of Japan's best experiences are simply walking around:

  • Shibuya Crossing in Tokyo — the famous scramble is free to experience.
  • Higashiyama and Gion in Kyoto — strolling the preserved old streets costs nothing.
  • Dotonbori in Osaka — the neon spectacle is free to soak up.
  • Arashiyama Bamboo Grove in Kyoto — walking the path is free.

Enjoy parks and gardens

Many public parks are free and beautiful, especially in cherry blossom and autumn seasons. Tokyo's large parks, Osaka Castle Park's grounds, and countless neighborhood green spaces make lovely, no-cost escapes. Some premium gardens charge a small fee, but plenty are free.

Catch a free view

You don't have to pay for observation decks. Some government and public buildings offer free observation floors with sweeping city views — a great budget alternative to paid towers. Department store rooftops and certain public spaces also provide good vantage points at no cost.

Explore markets

Browsing markets like Tokyo's Tsukiji Outer Market, Kyoto's Nishiki Market, or Osaka's Kuromon Market is free (though the food will tempt you). They're a feast for the senses and a window into local life.

More free experiences

  • People-watching in Harajuku or Akihabara.
  • Riverside and waterfront walks.
  • Window-shopping in electronics and department stores.
  • Seasonal festivals (many are free to attend).
  • Simply riding the trains and watching the country roll by.

Bottom line

Between free shrines, walkable neighborhoods, public parks, no-cost views, and lively markets, you can fill a Japan trip with rich experiences that cost nothing. Pair these with the occasional paid highlight, and Japan becomes far more affordable than its reputation suggests.

title: Hakone Day Trip Guide: Hot Springs and Mt Fuji Views
excerpt: Hakone is the classic mountain escape from Tokyo — onsen, Mt Fuji views, and a scenic loop of railways and boats. Here's how to do it.
content:
Hakone is the go-to mountain and hot-spring escape from Tokyo, famous for its onsen, scenic landscapes, and — on clear days — postcard views of Mt Fuji. It's close enough for a day trip, though an overnight in a ryokan makes it even better. Here's how to approach it.

What makes Hakone special

Hakone combines several attractions into one scenic area: natural hot springs (onsen), volcanic valleys, a beautiful lake, art museums, and views of Mt Fuji. The fun is partly in how you get around — a loop of charming mountain transport that's an experience in itself.

The classic Hakone loop

A typical day strings together several scenic modes of transport:

  • Mountain railway that switchbacks up the hillside.
  • Ropeway (cable car) gliding over Owakudani, a steaming volcanic valley where you can try the famous black eggs cooked in the hot springs.
  • Sightseeing boat (often pirate-ship themed) across scenic Lake Ashi, with Mt Fuji views on clear days.
  • Buses and trains connecting the pieces.

A regional pass covering this transport can save money and hassle if you're doing the full loop.

Highlights to add

  • Soak in an onsen: the whole point of Hakone for many — many ryokan and day-use baths are available.
  • Hakone Open-Air Museum: a celebrated sculpture park blending art and mountain scenery.
  • Hakone Shrine: with its iconic torii gate standing in Lake Ashi.
  • Owakudani: the dramatic volcanic valley and its black eggs.

Day trip or overnight?

Hakone is doable as a day trip from Tokyo, especially if you focus on the scenic loop and a day-use onsen. But to truly relax — and to maximize Fuji-viewing chances across morning and evening — an overnight ryokan stay is wonderful. If your schedule allows, one night in a Hakone onsen ryokan is a trip highlight.

Tips for clear Fuji views

Mt Fuji is famously shy, often hidden by clouds. To improve your odds, check the weather forecast and aim for a clear day; mornings and the colder, clearer months tend to offer better visibility. Don't count on the view, but when it appears, it's magical.

Practical notes

  • Start early to fit the full loop into a day.
  • Consider a regional transport pass for the railways, ropeway, and boat.
  • Bring layers — it's cooler in the mountains than in Tokyo.
  • Guided tours exist if you'd rather not navigate the connections yourself.

title: Nara Day Trip Guide: Deer and a Giant Buddha
excerpt: Nara is the easiest, most charming day trip from Kyoto or Osaka — free-roaming deer, a giant bronze Buddha, and ancient temples. Here's how to visit.
content:
Nara is one of Japan's most delightful day trips — easy to reach from Kyoto or Osaka, compact, and home to a giant bronze Buddha plus a park full of famously friendly deer. As Japan's capital even before Kyoto, it's rich in history and a favorite of travelers of every age. Here's how to do it.

The deer of Nara Park

Nara's most beloved attraction is its free-roaming deer, which wander the large central park and are considered sacred. You can buy special deer crackers (shika senbei) from vendors to feed them, and many of the deer have famously learned to bow for a treat. They're wild animals, so be gentle and follow the posted guidance — but interacting with them is a genuine highlight, especially for families.

Todai-ji and the Great Buddha

Todai-ji is Nara's crowning sight — a vast wooden temple housing an enormous bronze Buddha statue, one of the largest in Japan. The scale of both the hall and the Buddha is awe-inspiring. It's an easy walk through the deer park to reach it, and the temple is the centerpiece of any Nara visit.

More to see

  • Kasuga Taisha: a beautiful shrine famous for its hundreds of bronze and stone lanterns, set in the forest.
  • Kofuku-ji: a historic temple with a striking five-story pagoda near the park.
  • Nara Park itself: lovely for a relaxed stroll, with grassy expanses and woodland.
  • Naramachi: a preserved old merchant district with traditional shops and cafes.

How to do it

Nara is the easiest and closest of the Kansai day trips, reachable in well under an hour by train from Kyoto or Osaka. Most of the main sights are clustered around Nara Park within walking distance of each other, so it's an easy, low-stress day. A half-day covers the highlights; a full day lets you explore at a relaxed pace.

Practical tips

  • Start in the morning to enjoy the park before it gets busy.
  • Buy deer crackers from official vendors; don't feed the deer other food.
  • Be calm and gentle around the deer — they can get pushy when they smell crackers.
  • Wear comfortable shoes; it's a walkable but spread-out park.
  • Most sights are close together, so you won't need much transport once there.

Bottom line

For history, a giant Buddha, and the joy of bowing deer, Nara is an easy and rewarding day trip that almost every first-timer loves. If you have a spare day from Kyoto or Osaka, it's the one to choose.

title: Nikko Day Trip Guide: Shrines in the Forest
excerpt: Nikko offers spectacular UNESCO shrines among cedar forests and mountain scenery, a rewarding day trip north of Tokyo. Here's how to visit.
content:
Nikko is a mountain town north of Tokyo, celebrated for its spectacular UNESCO World Heritage shrines and temples set among towering cedar forests, plus waterfalls and lake scenery nearby. It's a rewarding day trip for travelers who love history and nature. Here's how to approach it.

The shrines and temples

Nikko's centerpiece is its complex of ornate shrines and temples, the most famous being Toshogu Shrine. Unlike the usual restraint of Japanese architecture, Toshogu is lavishly decorated — a riot of intricate carving, gold leaf, and color, including famous carved panels. The complex sits among ancient cedars, giving it a majestic, atmospheric setting. Exploring the shrines is the heart of a Nikko visit.

Nature beyond the shrines

If you have time and venture further, the area around Nikko offers beautiful natural scenery — mountain landscapes, waterfalls, and a scenic lake region up in the highlands. These take additional travel time from the shrine area, so a full day or overnight helps if you want both the shrines and the nature.

How to do it

Nikko is reachable from Tokyo by train, taking a bit longer than closer day trips like Kamakura, so it makes for a fuller day out. Many travelers focus on the shrine complex, which is walkable once you arrive, and add nearby nature only if time allows. Starting early maximizes what you can see.

Highlights checklist

  • Toshogu Shrine: the ornate, gold-adorned centerpiece.
  • Surrounding temples and shrines: the wider UNESCO complex among the cedars.
  • Shinkyo Bridge: a picturesque red bridge near the entrance to the shrine area.
  • Highland nature (with extra time): waterfalls and lake scenery in the mountains above town.

Practical tips

  • Start early — the travel time means you'll want a full day.
  • Consider a regional pass if available for the train and local buses.
  • Dress in layers; the mountains are cooler than Tokyo, and it can be snowy in winter.
  • Wear comfortable shoes for walking the forested shrine grounds.
  • Guided tours are available if you prefer not to handle the logistics.

Bottom line

Nikko rewards the longer journey with some of Japan's most spectacular shrine architecture in a stunning forest setting. For history and nature lovers willing to make a full day of it, it's one of the most memorable day trips from Tokyo.

title: Senso-ji Temple Guide (Asakusa, Tokyo)
excerpt: Senso-ji is Tokyo's oldest and most famous temple. Here's what to see, when to go, and how to make the most of your visit.
content:
Senso-ji, in Tokyo's Asakusa district, is the city's oldest and most famous temple, and one of its essential sights. With its grand gates, bustling approach, and historic atmosphere, it's the best place to experience old Tokyo. Here's a guide to visiting.

What you'll see

Kaminarimon (Thunder Gate)

Your visit begins at the iconic Kaminarimon, the outer gate famous for its enormous red paper lantern. It's one of Tokyo's most photographed landmarks and the symbolic entrance to the temple.

Nakamise shopping street

Beyond the gate stretches Nakamise, a lively shopping street lined with stalls selling traditional snacks, sweets, and souvenirs. It's a fun, atmospheric walk up to the temple — grab a freshly made treat along the way.

The main hall and grounds

At the end of Nakamise stands the second gate and the grand main hall. You'll find a large incense burner where visitors waft the smoke for good fortune, and a five-story pagoda nearby. The grounds are atmospheric and free to explore.

When to go

Senso-ji is popular and can be very crowded midday. For the best experience, visit early in the morning before the crowds, or in the evening when the temple and gates are beautifully illuminated and far quieter. Both times are magical and much more pleasant than the midday crush.

Combine with nearby sights

Senso-ji sits in Asakusa, an area full of traditional charm — wander the backstreets for craft shops and old eateries. Just across the river rises Tokyo Skytree, an easy add-on for sweeping views. Together they make a perfect half-day combining old and new Tokyo.

Etiquette and tips

  • Be respectful — it's an active place of worship as well as a tourist site.
  • You can observe or take part in customs like wafting incense smoke or drawing a fortune (omikuji).
  • The grounds are free; carry small change for snacks, charms, or fortunes.
  • Photography is fine in general areas; be mindful inside halls and of worshippers.
  • It's walkable and well connected by subway.

Bottom line

Senso-ji is a Tokyo must-see that captures the city's traditional soul. Visit early or in the evening to enjoy it at its best, savor the Nakamise street snacks, and pair it with Skytree for a memorable half-day in old Tokyo.

title: Fushimi Inari Shrine Guide (Kyoto)
excerpt: Fushimi Inari's thousands of red torii gates are one of Japan's most iconic sights. Here's how to visit, when to go, and what to expect.
content:
Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyoto is one of Japan's most iconic and photographed sights — a shrine famous for its thousands of vermilion torii gates forming tunnels up a wooded mountainside. Walking through them is an unforgettable experience. Here's how to make the most of a visit.

What makes it special

Fushimi Inari is the head shrine of Inari, and its hallmark is the seemingly endless rows of torii gates — donated over the years — that wind in bright orange-red tunnels up the mountain. The effect of walking beneath them is mesmerizing and unlike anywhere else. The shrine also features fox statues, regarded as messengers of Inari.

The hike up the mountain

The full trail climbs the mountain and takes a couple of hours round trip, passing through gate corridors, smaller shrines, and viewpoints over Kyoto. You do not have to do the whole thing — even walking a portion of the way up rewards you with the iconic gate tunnels. Go as far as you like and turn back when you wish; the densest, most famous gates are in the lower sections.

When to go

Fushimi Inari is extremely popular, so timing matters. Visit early in the morning or later in the evening to experience the gates with fewer crowds — the shrine grounds are open and accessible, and it's even atmospheric (and lit in parts) after dark. Midday can be very crowded in the lower sections. It's also free to enter.

Practical tips

  • Wear comfortable shoes — the mountain trail involves a lot of steps.
  • Bring water, especially in warm weather, for the climb.
  • Go early to beat both crowds and heat.
  • It's easy to reach by train from central Kyoto.
  • The higher you go, the thinner the crowds become.

Combine with your day

Fushimi Inari is on the southern/eastern side of Kyoto, making it a natural pairing with a day exploring the eastern Higashiyama district and Kiyomizu-dera. Many travelers start at Fushimi Inari early, then move on to other eastern sights. It fits neatly into a Kyoto temple day.

Bottom line

The torii-gate tunnels of Fushimi Inari are a quintessential Japan experience and a first-trip essential. Go early or late, walk as far up as you like, wear good shoes, and enjoy one of the country's most magical sights — for free.

title: Meiji Shrine Guide (Tokyo)
excerpt: Meiji Shrine is a tranquil forest sanctuary in the heart of Tokyo, beside busy Harajuku. Here's what to see and how to visit respectfully.
content:
Meiji Shrine (Meiji Jingu) is one of Tokyo's most important and serene Shinto shrines, set in a tranquil forest right beside the bustle of Harajuku and Shibuya. The contrast — deep calm a stone's throw from the city's busiest youth district — is what makes it special. Here's how to visit.

A forest in the city

The shrine sits within a large wooded area of trees planted to create a peaceful sanctuary. The approach takes you along gravel paths beneath towering trees and through grand wooden torii gates, leaving the city noise behind. The walk through the forest to the shrine is a meditative experience in itself.

What to see

  • The grand torii gates: impressive wooden gates marking the sacred approach.
  • The main shrine buildings: elegant and understated, in classic Shinto style, around a peaceful courtyard.
  • Sake and wine barrel displays: decorative offerings lining part of the approach.
  • Seasonal gardens: an inner garden (small fee) is lovely, especially when irises bloom.

Experience the customs

Meiji Shrine is an active place of worship, and you may see traditional ceremonies, and sometimes wedding processions in traditional dress. Visitors are welcome to take part in customs: cleanse your hands at the water pavilion, make an offering, and offer a prayer at the main hall (the typical etiquette is two bows, two claps, one bow). Writing a wish on a wooden plaque (ema) is another option.

When to go and how

The shrine is free to enter (the inner garden has a small fee) and open during daylight hours. It's right next to Harajuku, making it incredibly easy to combine with a visit to Takeshita Street, Omotesando, and Shibuya. Mornings are especially peaceful. Allow an hour or so for the forest walk and shrine.

Etiquette and tips

  • Be quiet and respectful, especially near the main hall and during ceremonies.
  • Bow when passing through the torii gates if you wish to observe custom.
  • Follow the hand-washing ritual at the purification fountain.
  • Photography is generally fine in the grounds; be discreet around worshippers and ceremonies.
  • Comfortable shoes help for the gravel forest paths.

Bottom line

Meiji Shrine offers a serene, spiritual counterpoint to Tokyo's energy, and its location beside Harajuku makes it effortless to visit. Take the peaceful forest walk, observe or join the customs respectfully, and enjoy one of the city's most tranquil and meaningful sights.

title: Temple and Shrine Etiquette in Japan
excerpt: How to behave respectfully at Japan's temples and shrines — purification, prayer customs, photography, and the key dos and don'ts for visitors.
content:
Visiting Japan's temples and shrines is a highlight of any trip, and a little etiquette goes a long way toward showing respect. The customs are simple and locals are gracious with visitors who make an effort. Here's what to know.

Temples vs shrines

First, a quick distinction: shrines are Shinto and marked by torii gates; temples are Buddhist and often have large gates with guardian statues and incense burners. The etiquette overlaps but differs slightly, as noted below. Both are active places of worship as well as sights.

At a Shinto shrine

  • Torii gates: it's customary to bow slightly when passing through, and to avoid walking down the exact center of the path, which is considered the way of the gods.
  • Purify yourself: at the water pavilion (temizuya) near the entrance, use the ladle to rinse your hands (and symbolically your mouth) before approaching.
  • Praying: at the main hall, the common custom is to make a small offering, then bow twice, clap twice, make your wish/prayer, and bow once more.

At a Buddhist temple

  • Incense: you may waft the smoke from a large burner toward yourself for good fortune and health.
  • Praying: make an offering and pray quietly with hands together — without clapping (clapping is for shrines, not temples).
  • Shoes: remove them where indicated before entering temple buildings.

General respect

  • Keep your voice down and behave calmly — these are sacred spaces.
  • Dress reasonably modestly, especially at the most sacred sites.
  • Don't touch statues, artifacts, or ritual objects unless clearly invited to.
  • Follow any posted rules about specific areas.

Photography

Photography is usually fine in outdoor grounds, but often restricted or prohibited inside main halls and around certain sacred objects — watch for signs. Always be discreet and respectful when worshippers or ceremonies are present; don't photograph people praying up close without consideration.

Small practical notes

  • Carry small change and coins for offerings, charms (omamori), and fortunes (omikuji).
  • Many sites have small entry fees for inner areas or gardens, especially temples.
  • If you draw a fortune you don't like, there are often racks to tie it and leave it behind.
  • Opening hours are often limited to daylight; plan accordingly.

Bottom line

The key is simple: be quiet, be respectful, purify before praying at shrines, remember clapping is for shrines not temples, and mind photography rules inside halls. Make a genuine effort and you'll be warmly received — and your temple and shrine visits will be all the more meaningful.

title: Kamakura Day Trip Guide: The Great Buddha by the Sea
excerpt: Kamakura is an easy, relaxed coastal day trip from Tokyo, famous for its open-air Great Buddha, temples, and beaches. Here's how to visit.
content:
Kamakura is a relaxed coastal town within easy reach of Tokyo, best known for its monumental open-air Great Buddha, along with atmospheric temples, shrines, and a seaside setting. It's the most laid-back of the classic Tokyo day trips and a lovely change of pace. Here's how to do it.

The Great Buddha (Daibutsu)

Kamakura's signature sight is the Great Buddha, a massive bronze statue seated serenely in the open air at Kotoku-in temple. Once housed in a hall that was washed away centuries ago, it has sat outdoors ever since, which only adds to its presence. Standing before it is a quietly awe-inspiring experience and the centerpiece of any visit.

Temples and shrines

Kamachura was once Japan's political capital, and it's dotted with historic temples and shrines:

  • Hase-dera: a beautiful temple with gardens, sea views, and a revered Kannon statue, near the Great Buddha.
  • Tsurugaoka Hachimangu: the town's grand central shrine, reached via a long approach with torii gates.
  • Numerous smaller temples scattered through the hills, some along pleasant hiking trails.

The seaside

Being a coastal town, Kamachura has beaches that are popular in summer, and a generally breezy, relaxed atmosphere. The nearby area of Enoshima, a small island with a shrine and views, makes a scenic add-on if you have time, often reached by a charming local train along the coast.

How to do it

Kamakura is easy and close — about an hour from Tokyo by train — making it one of the simplest day trips. The main sights are reachable by local train and some walking, and a relaxed half-day to full day covers the highlights. Its proximity and laid-back vibe make it ideal if you want temples plus sea air without venturing far.

Practical tips

  • Start in the morning to enjoy the sights at a relaxed pace.
  • Wear comfortable shoes — there's walking between sights, some uphill.
  • The local coastal train (Enoden) is scenic and fun for getting around.
  • Combine the Great Buddha and Hase-dera, which are close together.
  • Carry small change for temple entry fees.

Bottom line

For an easy, scenic day trip combining a magnificent Buddha, historic temples, and sea air, Kamakura is hard to beat. Its proximity to Tokyo and relaxed coastal charm make it a refreshing and rewarding escape from the city.

title: Himeji Castle Day Trip Guide
excerpt: Himeji Castle is Japan's finest original castle, an easy Shinkansen trip from Kyoto or Osaka. Here's what to see and how to plan your visit.
content:
Himeji Castle is widely regarded as Japan's most spectacular castle — a brilliant white hilltop fortress nicknamed the "White Heron" for its elegant, soaring form. Unlike many Japanese castles that are modern reconstructions, Himeji is an original, and a UNESCO World Heritage site. It makes a rewarding day trip from Kyoto or Osaka. Here's how to visit.

Why Himeji is special

Most castles you'll see in Japan are 20th-century concrete rebuilds. Himeji is the real thing — a genuinely old wooden castle that survived wars and time, beautifully preserved. Its gleaming white walls, layered roofs, and elegant silhouette make it the finest example of Japanese castle architecture, and a UNESCO World Heritage site. For history and architecture lovers, it's a must.

What to see

  • The main keep: you can climb up through its wooden interior floors, seeing the defensive design — steep stairs, weapon racks, and views from the top.
  • The defensive layout: the maze-like approach paths, gates, and walls were designed to confound attackers; walking them is fascinating.
  • Koko-en Garden: a beautiful adjacent Japanese garden, often combined with a castle ticket.
  • The grounds: gorgeous in cherry blossom season, when the white castle is framed by pink blooms.

How to get there

Himeji is farther than the closer Kansai day trips, but the Shinkansen makes it very manageable — the bullet train reaches Himeji efficiently from Kyoto or Osaka, and the castle is a straightforward walk from the station along a grand avenue (you'll see it ahead of you). A Japan Rail Pass or regional pass can make the fares more economical.

How long to spend

Himeji works as a half-day to full-day trip. The castle itself takes a couple of hours to explore properly (more if it's busy, as climbing the keep can involve queues), plus time for the garden. It can also be combined with other stops for a fuller day out.

Practical tips

  • Arrive early, especially in peak season — climbing the keep can get crowded and entry is sometimes limited at busy times.
  • Wear socks and easy-off shoes; you remove shoes to climb the wooden keep.
  • The stairs inside are steep and narrow — wear comfortable clothing.
  • Combine your ticket with Koko-en Garden next door.
  • Cherry blossom season is stunning but very busy.

Bottom line

For Japan's grandest and most authentic castle, Himeji is well worth the Shinkansen ride. Its dazzling white form, fascinating defensive design, and UNESCO status make it a standout day trip for anyone interested in Japan's history and architecture.

title: Best Things to Do in Japan: Top Experiences for First-Timers
excerpt: From bullet trains to onsen to temple towns, here are the top experiences every first-time visitor to Japan should have on their list.
content:
Japan offers an incredible range of experiences, from ancient traditions to futuristic cities. If it's your first trip, here are the top things to do — the experiences that capture what makes Japan special and belong on any first-timer's list.

Ride the Shinkansen

The bullet train is an experience in itself — gliding between cities at high speed, punctual to the minute, comfortable and smooth. The classic Tokyo-to-Kyoto run is a rite of passage. Don't think of it as just transport; it's one of the quintessential things to do in Japan.

Soak in an onsen

Bathing in a natural hot spring is deeply woven into Japanese culture and a blissful experience, especially outdoors in a scenic setting or at a traditional ryokan. Once you learn the simple etiquette, an onsen soak is pure relaxation and a trip highlight.

Explore Tokyo and Kyoto

Experience the contrast at the heart of Japan: electric, futuristic Tokyo with its neon, food, and energy, and serene, traditional Kyoto with its temples, shrines, and old streets. Together they show the country's two faces and anchor nearly every first trip.

Visit temples and shrines

From Kyoto's golden Kinkaku-ji and the torii tunnels of Fushimi Inari to Tokyo's Senso-ji and the giant Buddha at Nara, Japan's temples and shrines are essential — spiritual, beautiful, and often free to enter.

Eat your way across the country

Japanese food is a destination in itself: slurp ramen, savor sushi, graze street food in Osaka's Dotonbori, settle into an izakaya, and try a refined kaiseki meal. Eating well is one of the great joys of a Japan trip — and remember, no tipping.

Stay in a ryokan

Spend at least one night in a traditional ryokan — tatami rooms, futon bedding, a hot-spring bath, and a multi-course dinner. It's a cultural experience that turns a place to sleep into a memory.

See Mt Fuji

Catch a glimpse of iconic Mt Fuji, whether from the Shinkansen window, a Hakone viewpoint, or a lakeside town on a clear day. Japan's most famous symbol is a thrill to see in person.

Experience the seasons

Time your trip for cherry blossoms in spring or autumn foliage in fall, when Japan's landscapes and temples are at their most beautiful. The seasonal spectacle is unforgettable.

More memorable experiences

  • Take a day trip — Nara's deer, Hakone's hot springs, Himeji's castle.
  • Wander a neon nightlife district or a quiet bamboo grove.
  • Visit teamLab's immersive digital art in Tokyo.
  • Browse a bustling food market.
  • Simply soak up the safety, cleanliness, and kindness that define daily life in Japan.

Bottom line

The best things to do in Japan blend the modern and the traditional — bullet trains and onsen, neon cities and ancient temples, incredible food and natural beauty. Build your first trip around these experiences and you'll come away understanding exactly why travelers fall in love with Japan.
